catalog_quote: Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word. Examples of stress assignment to the root-final syllable are provided for verbs and nouns in (7-8) and (9-10), respectively. In nouns, this stress pattern is a bit obscured as they always surface with the extrametrical nominalizing enclitic =a. On the surface, then, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of nouns bearing the enclitic =a. (7) /ɛ-pi/ → [ɛ.ˈpi] ‘Shut off!’ (8) /ɛ-kɨtʃi/ → [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi] ‘Cut (it)!’ (9) /janu=a/ → [ñã.ˈndu.a] ‘spider’ (10) /tapiʔiɾ=a/ → [ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa] ‘tapir’ However, some suffixes trigger stress shift from the root-final syllable, both in verbs and nouns. For instance, stress remains on the final syllable of the verb root in (11) after circumfixation of the sentential negation nd(a)-…-i, but shifts in (12) after suffixation of -ahim ‘very’. Another suffix that triggers stress shift is -uhu ‘aug’ (13-14). Examples (15)-(16) provide evidence of stress shift due to suffixation in nouns. (11) /n-aimɛ-i/ → [nd-aĩˈmbɛ-i] ‘be dull’ (12) /aimɛ-ahim/ → [aĩmbɛ-aˈhĩm] ‘be very sharp’ (13) /i-ipi/ → [j-iˈpi] ‘be dark’ (14) /i-ipi-uhu/ → [j-ipi-uˈhu] ‘be very dark’ (15) /vɨɾa=a/ → [vɨˈɾa] ‘bird’ (16) /vɨɾa-ʔi=a/ → [vɨɾaˈʔia] ‘small bird’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the lexical root. The obligatory nominalizing enclitic =a is extrametrical, so surface nouns are penultimate-stressed ([ñã.ˈndu.a], [ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa]) while bare verb forms are final-stressed ([ɛ.ˈpi], [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi]). The negation circumfix nd(a)-..-i does not take stress ([nd-aĩˈmbɛ-i]); a listed set of suffixes (-ahim 'very', -uhu 'aug', diminutive -ʔi) attract stress onto themselves ([aĩmbɛ-aˈhĩm], [j-ipi-uˈhu], [vɨɾaˈʔia]). No syllable-weight conditioning and no tone are described; the oral/nasal vowel contrast is confined to the stressed root-final syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described (no statement on secondary or rhythmic stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Extrametrical =a 'nmlz' (penultimate surface stress in nouns); neg circumfix -i unstressed; stress-attracting suffixes -ahim, -uhu, -ʔi. Sec. 4.5 (syntax) additionally notes that the verb and a following C-head particle each bear their own stress, i.e. do not form one prosodic word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over the morphological word ('root-final syllable of a word'); examples are citation/elicited forms with morpheme glosses. Analysis explicitly based on the Juma and Jupaú (Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau) dialects of Kawahíva, with Jupaú consultants named (Tangãi and Awip Uru Eu Wau Wau).
new_statements.identity_note: dos Santos 2024 treats Kawahíva as a single language with eight varieties and states that his phonological analysis (sec. 3.2) is 'based on the Juma and Jupaú dialects'; Jupaú = Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau (the dissertation's abbreviation list: 'uRz iso code for Jupaú (also known as Uru Eu Wau Wau)'), so the statement is first-hand for urue1240 (jointly with Juma, juma1249). The same file was already used as the deciding source for the sister variety Amundava (amun1246); the catalog should note that one statement covers both glottocodes. Marçoli 2018 (held by the project) gives a concurring root-final rule but only for Tenharim, Jiahui and Amondawa, not Jupaú. Vezzaro 2014 says Uru Eu Wau Wau 'conta com dois dialetos básicos – os Uru Eu Wau Wau, propriamente dito e os Amondáwa'; Netto & Moraes 1992, though titled Uru Eu Wau Wau, is subtitled 'subgrupo Mondáwa' (i.e. Amondawa).

new_statements.quote: Assim, o acento na língua UWW pode ocorrer na última e na penúltima sílaba, como mostram os seguintes exemplos: Na última sílaba: (1) /piˈra/ [piˈɾa] = peixe (2) /koˈp/ = tarde [...] Na penúltima sílaba: (5) /maˈtɾə/ = coisa [...] (7) /taˈpy’jə/ [taˈpɨjə] = casa. Portanto, para os autores, o acento é fonológico, previsível na língua, recaindo na última e/ou na penúltima sílaba. De acordo com os dados coletados para esse trabalho, foi possível observar um número muito maior de palavras paroxítonas [...] Somente será marcado nas oxítonas indicando a quebra do padrão acentual que, assume-se, preliminarmente, que é paroxítono no UWW, porém carece de um estudo mais detalhado fonológico
new_statements.translation: Thus, stress in the UWW language can occur on the last and on the penultimate syllable, as the following examples show: On the last syllable: (1) /piˈra/ 'fish' (2) /koˈp/ 'afternoon' [...] On the penultimate syllable: (5) /maˈtɾə/ 'thing' [...] (7) /taˈpɨjə/ 'house'. Therefore, for the authors [Ferreira Netto & Moraes 1992], stress is phonological, predictable in the language, falling on the last and/or the penultimate syllable. According to the data collected for this work, a much larger number of paroxytone words was observed [...] [Stress] will only be marked on oxytones, indicating a break in the stress pattern which is assumed, preliminarily, to be paroxytone in UWW, but this needs a more detailed phonological study.

new_statements.relation_note: Type differs from the catalog's existing statement (dos Santos 2024: stress on the root-final syllable, nominalizing enclitic =a extrametrical, some suffixes attract stress). Vezzaro posits a surface penultimate default with lexical oxytone exceptions. The underlying facts coincide: every penult example she cites is a noun ending in the nominal ə/-a that dos Santos treats as extrametrical ('On the surface, then, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of nouns bearing the enclitic =a', dos Santos p. 40), and her oxytones are C-final words or vowel-final roots. Her statement is avowedly preliminary and its data are second-hand (Ferreira Netto & Moraes 1992, Amondawa subgroup), so it does no…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Following Ferreira Netto & Moraes (1992), stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable; Vezzaro observes many more paroxytones in her data and preliminarily assumes a penultimate (paroxytone) default for Uru Eu Wau Wau, writing the accent only on oxytone words as exceptions, and explicitly contrasts this with the 'padrão acentual oxítono típico das línguas TG' (citing Dietrich 1986 on Parintintin as also paroxytone). She flags the statement as preliminary and in need of a dedicated phonological study. All her penult examples end in the unstressed central vowel ə (the nominal -a); her final-stress examples are consonant-/diphthong-final or the vowel-final root pira 'fish'.
new_statements.exceptions: Oxytone words (e.g. /piˈra/ 'peixe', /koˈp/ 'tarde', /eˈhõy/ 'grande', /moˈkõy/ 'dois') treated as marked exceptions to the assumed paroxytone pattern; no weight or morphological conditioning proposed.
new_statements.identity_note: Ferreira Netto & Moraes 1992 describes the Mondáwa (Amondawa) subgroup, Glottolog amun1246 Amundava [adw], not the Jupaú dialect; Vezzaro 2015's own consultants are Jupaú (Aldeias 621, 623, Alto Jamari, Jaru = urue1240 proper) but her stress paragraph rests on Netto & Moraes's Amondawa examples; dos Santos 2024's phonology is 'based on the Juma and Jupaú dialects'. All sources treat Jupaú, Amondawa, Tenharim/Parintintin and Juma as mutually intelligible varieties of one Kawahíva language.

readall_conflicts: The three sources agree on the surface distribution and disagree on the analysis. dos Santos 2024 (catalog; phonology based on Juma and Jupaú) derives everything from stress on the root-final syllable with the nominalizing enclitic =a extrametrical and a few stress-attracting suffixes (-ahim, -uhu, -ʔi). Ferreira Netto & Moraes 1992 (Amondawa subgroup, preliminary ms.) call stress distinctive, final or penultimate, with penult predominating in ə-final words and cite the pair 'peixe' vs 'pele' as a stress minimal pair; under dos Santos's analysis that pair is pira (vowel-final root, final stress) vs pir=a (root + extrametrical nominalizer, penult stress), so the contrast is morphological, not lexical. Vezzaro 2015 (Jupaú fieldwork, but her stress section reproduces Netto & Moraes's Amondawa data) goes further and preliminarily assumes a paroxytone default for Uru Eu Wau Wau, marking oxytones as exceptions and contrasting the language with the TG oxytone norm; this generalization conflicts with dos Santos's root-final rule for verbs and vowel-final roots (e.g. [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi] 'cut!', [vɨˈɾa] 'bird'), and she herself says it needs a proper phonological study. Sampaio 1998 (downloaded as context, Amondawa-based phonology) states explicitly that syllable and accent were not treated. Net: no factual disagreement about where stress is heard; the catalog's root-final (morphological) statement remains the best-supported analysis, with the older works documenting the surface penult patter…
